No reflection on what you learned

Steps you took in the first two weeks
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you lost a job or a major project unexpectedly.

pitfalls: A story with no conflict
Taking sole credit for team work
points: The disagreement and each side's view
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you disagreed with a manager or a client about direction.

pitfalls: Staying purely technical
No measurable result
points: The audience and what they cared about
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you influenced a decision without having authority.

pitfalls: Describing only the learning, not the delivery
No deadline pressure mentioned
points: What you had to learn and by when
How you applied it on the deadline
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to get up to speed on something completely new fast.

pitfalls: A vague 'we worked hard' story
No numbers on the improvement
points: What you changed in the process
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you improved a process, not just executed it.

pitfalls: Claiming you never fail
Blaming circumstances only
points: What went wrong and your part in it
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a professional failure and what it taught you.

pitfalls: Only the technical fix, no communication
No prevention follow-through

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you handled a high-pressure incident with a customer or user affected.

No action you took yourself

Who you sought out and what you asked

disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Vendor-neutral — not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

choices: Take the highest salary; money is the only objective measure
Take the startup; chaos always means faster growth
Score each offer on learning, trajectory, manager quality, and runway — then weigh salary inside that picture
Delay both and keep interviewing until a perfect offer appears
evidence: Startup: $128k, 60-hr weeks, 9 months runway, brilliant but stretched manager
Mid-size firm: $104k, 40-hr weeks, profitable, manager known for growing juniors into seniors
scenarios.hint: Salary is one term in a multi-year equation — which offer compounds your skills and options fastest over three years?
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest way to decide?
scenarios.situation: You hold two offers: a chaotic startup at $128k with 9 months of runway, and a stable mid-size firm at $104k with a manager famous for developing people.
scenarios.title: The two-offer dilemma
scenarios.why: Early-career earnings compound through skills, not starting salary: a great manager and sustainable pace usually beat a 20% premium at a chaotic shop. Score offers on learning velocity, manager quality, financial stability, and trajectory — then let salary be one weighted factor, not the whole decision.

choices: Leave the gap off the resume and hope nobody asks
Name it plainly: contract project work plus deliberate upskilling, with specifics
Call it consulting to sound employed the whole time
Blame the market and move on quickly
scenarios.hint: Interviewers can smell euphemism — what happens to trust when the plain truth is actually a reasonable story?
scenarios.prompt: How should you address the 14-month gap?
scenarios.situation: Your resume shows a 14-month gap: six months of contract gigs plus eight months of full-time study (certifications, open-source contributions).
scenarios.title: The resume gap
scenarios.why: Name it plainly with specifics: 'contract support work plus full-time upskilling — here are the certs and the repos.' Euphemisms ('consulting') invite verification problems; a factual, forward-looking framing turns the gap into evidence of initiative. Never lie — background checks end careers faster than gaps do.

choices: Translate past wins into the new field's language: 'I kept 200 users productive through three migrations' becomes reliability engineering
Start over as if the past decade did not happen
List every tool you have ever touched to look versatile
Apply only to senior titles to protect your salary history
evidence: 10 years IT support, now targeting DevOps roles
scenarios.hint: Hiring managers buy outcomes, not tool lists — which of your past outcomes already is a DevOps outcome?
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest pivot strategy?
scenarios.situation: After ten years in IT support, you are targeting DevOps roles. Your resume reads like a help-desk history.
scenarios.title: The support-to-DevOps pivot
scenarios.why: Translate outcomes into the target field's vocabulary: uptime kept, incidents resolved, scripts that automated toil — that is already reliability work. Pair it with proof of the delta (a homelab pipeline, a cert, shipped automation). Tool-list stuffing and title inflation both fail the first technical screen.

choices: Apply to 200 jobs; it is purely a numbers game
Only apply where you meet 100% of the requirements
Get a warm introduction, then apply through the front door so your resume is expected
Ask the contact to forward your resume with no context
evidence: Referral hires: ~30-50% of hires from ~7% of applicants (industry pattern)
scenarios.hint: A referral is not a favor — it is information. What does the referrer need to be able to say about you truthfully?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective way to use a connection at a target company?
scenarios.situation: A former colleague works at a company you want to join. A referral dramatically improves your odds.
scenarios.title: The warm introduction
scenarios.why: Ask for a 15-minute call first: learn the team's real problems, then let them refer you with specifics ('she automated exactly the migration pain we have'). A context-free forward is a weak signal; an informed referral is a strong one. And always apply through the portal too — make yourself easy to hire.

choices: Accept the first offer; negotiating risks it being pulled
Anchor with researched range data and trade across the whole package
Give an ultimatum number and walk away if unmet
Share your current salary so they can 'be fair'
evidence: Market range for the role in your city: $95k-$120k. Offer: $92k.
scenarios.hint: Negotiation is collaborative problem-solving, not combat — what information makes your ask feel reasonable rather than aggressive?
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest negotiation move?
scenarios.situation: You receive a $92k offer; your research says the market range is $95k–$120k for this role in your city.
scenarios.title: The low offer
scenarios.why: Counter with data: 'Based on market data for this role here, I was expecting $105k–$115k — can we bridge the gap, including signing bonus or extra PTO?' Anchoring on research keeps it collaborative; ultimatums and current-salary disclosures both weaken you. And yes — negotiated offers are very rarely pulled for a polite, data-backed counter.

choices: File for unemployment, lock a daily routine, and activate your network in week one
Take a month off to decompress before thinking about it
Immediately mass-apply to everything, anywhere
Tell no one; job searching is private
evidence: Laid off Friday. Severance: 2 weeks. Savings: 3 months.
scenarios.hint: A layoff is a project with a deadline — what are the highest-leverage actions in the first seven days?
scenarios.prompt: What should the first week look like?
scenarios.situation: You were laid off on Friday with two weeks' severance and three months of savings.
scenarios.title: The layoff week one
scenarios.why: Week one: file unemployment, set a daily structure (search is a job), tell your network immediately — most roles are filled through connections, and speed matters because employed contacts forget. Mass-applying burns you out; hiding the layoff starves you of leads. Treat it as a project: pipeline, metrics, weekly review.

choices: Keep talking; detail shows competence
Apologize and restart from the beginning
Pause, summarize the outcome first, then offer the 60-second STAR version
Ask the interviewer to repeat the question
evidence: Q: 'Tell me about a conflict at work.' A: 6 minutes on team history, no conflict described yet...
scenarios.hint: Interviewers remember structure, not sprawl — what skeleton turns a story into an answer?
scenarios.prompt: You are four minutes into a rambling answer. What is the best recovery?
scenarios.situation: Mid-answer you realize you have been talking for four minutes about team history without reaching the point.
scenarios.title: The rambling answer
scenarios.why: Pause and re-anchor: 'Let me land this — the situation was X, I did Y, the result was Z.' STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) in 60–90 seconds beats six minutes of context. Interviewers forgive a pause; they penalize answers that never land.

choices: Name a real, non-fatal weakness and show the system you built to manage it
Say you have no weaknesses
Offer a disguised strength: 'I work too hard'
Pick a weakness unrelated to the job so it cannot hurt you
scenarios.hint: The interviewer is testing self-awareness, not perfection — what answer proves you can see yourself clearly?
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest answer?
scenarios.situation: The interviewer asks the classic weakness question.
scenarios.title: The weakness question
scenarios.why: 'I used to avoid difficult conversations, so I started a practice of writing the hard message within 24 hours — my last two performance reviews noted the improvement.' Real weakness, owned, with a mitigation system and evidence. 'No weaknesses' signals no self-awareness; humblebrags insult the interviewer's intelligence.

choices: Go silent until the answer comes to you
Think aloud: restate the problem, ask a clarifying question, and narrate your approach
Guess quickly to show decisiveness
Say 'I don't know' and stop
evidence: Design a rate limiter. Candidate stares silently for 90 seconds.
scenarios.hint: The interviewer cannot grade a silent mind — what turns your thinking into something they can evaluate?
scenarios.prompt: What is the best move when you are stuck?
scenarios.situation: Ninety seconds into a system-design question, your mind is blank.
scenarios.title: The blank whiteboard
scenarios.why: Narrate: 'Let me restate the requirements — 10k requests per second per user... First I'd clarify burst vs sustained...' Thinking aloud converts a blank into a collaboration; clarifying questions buy time and often reveal the intended path. Silence is ungradeable; a narrated partial approach frequently passes.

choices: Ask about perks and remote-work policy first
Ask nothing; it suggests you are easy to please
Ask about success metrics, team challenges, and what the manager's reports say about them
Ask how fast you can get promoted
evidence: 'What questions do you have for us?' — 10 minutes left
scenarios.hint: Your questions are a second interview — what do they reveal about how you think?
scenarios.prompt: Which questions make the strongest impression?
scenarios.situation: The interviewer turns it over: 'What questions do you have for us?'
scenarios.title: The flipped interview
scenarios.why: 'What does success look like in 90 days? What's the hardest problem the team faces right now? What do your reports say working for you is like?' These signal you evaluate jobs like an owner and surface real information. Perk-first questions signal you are shopping; no questions signal you are not.

choices: Send a concise thank-you within 24 hours referencing something specific from the conversation
Send a long recap of your qualifications immediately
Wait a week so you don't seem desperate
Connect on LinkedIn with no message the same evening
scenarios.hint: The note has two jobs: gratitude and memory — what makes an interviewer remember you on Friday?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right follow-up?
scenarios.situation: Your final interview ended Tuesday at 3pm.
scenarios.title: The thank-you note
scenarios.why: Within 24 hours, send 3–4 sentences: thanks, one specific thing you enjoyed discussing, brief reaffirmation of fit. Specificity ('your approach to incident reviews') beats generic flattery and keeps you memorable during debriefs. Long recaps get skimmed; silence is forgettable.

choices: Name the first number that comes to mind
Deflect to a researched range: 'Based on market data, I'm looking at $X-$Y depending on the full package'
Refuse to discuss money until an offer exists
State your current salary and ask for 10% more
evidence: 'What are your salary expectations?' — first interview
scenarios.hint: Early in the process, precision hurts you and vagueness wastes time — what threads the needle?
scenarios.prompt: How should you answer in a first interview?
scenarios.situation: The recruiter asks your salary expectations in the screening call.
scenarios.title: The salary question
scenarios.why: A researched range ('market data puts this at $105k–$120k; I'm targeting the middle depending on the package') keeps you in the running without anchoring low. Naming a single number early either prices you out or leaves money behind; refusing entirely stalls the process. Save hard negotiation for the written offer.

choices: Take a personality quiz and adopt its labels
Collect evidence: what do people repeatedly thank you for, and where do you outperform with less effort?
Ask your manager to tell you your strengths
List what you enjoy; enjoyment equals strength
evidence: 3 years of peer feedback mention 'calm in incidents' and 'explains clearly'
scenarios.hint: Strengths leave a trail — what pattern repeats across years of feedback?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most reliable way to identify your real strengths?
scenarios.situation: You are rewriting your resume and realize you cannot articulate what you are actually great at.
scenarios.title: The strengths audit
scenarios.why: Strengths show up as repeated external evidence: the thanks you keep getting, the tasks where you outperform with less strain. Quizzes label you; enjoyment misleads (you can love things you are mediocre at). Mine three years of reviews and peer thanks for patterns — that is your strengths list.

choices: Maximize prestige; values are a luxury
Take whichever pays most and adjust your values later
Rank your non-negotiables (e.g., autonomy, stability, mission) and score the options against them
Follow what your peers are choosing
evidence: A: prestigious, 60-hr weeks, work you find meaningless. B: modest, 40 hrs, mission you believe in.
scenarios.hint: Regret usually comes from violating your own values, not from missing prestige — which choice will you defend to yourself in five years?
scenarios.prompt: How should you decide?
scenarios.situation: Two paths: prestigious but draining and meaningless, or modest but aligned with what you believe.
scenarios.title: The values tradeoff
scenarios.why: Write your non-negotiables first — autonomy, stability, craft, mission — then score honestly. People rarely regret choosing alignment; they routinely regret prestige that cost their health or integrity. Values are decision criteria, not decorations.

choices: Treat it as data: cynicism, dread, and exhaustion are signals to investigate workload, autonomy, or meaning
Push harder; burnout is just weakness
Quit immediately without a plan
Blame your manager and disengage quietly
evidence: Sunday dread, snapping at teammates, work that used to energize now numbs
scenarios.hint: Burnout is information about the fit between you and the work — what is it information about, specifically?
scenarios.prompt: What is the healthiest first response?
scenarios.situation: Sunday dread, snapping at teammates, and numbness about work that used to energize you.
scenarios.title: The burnout signals
scenarios.why: Name it as data, then diagnose: is it volume (too much), control (no autonomy), or meaning (pointless work)? Each has a different fix — boundaries, a conversation, or an exit plan. 'Push harder' deepens it; quiet quitting spreads it to the team. Treat the signal seriously and early.

choices: Defend yourself point by point in the moment
Listen fully, ask clarifying questions, and separate the signal from the sting before responding
Agree with everything to end the discomfort
Dismiss it; they don't understand your work
evidence: 'Your updates are too detailed; stakeholders tune out.'
scenarios.hint: Feedback is a gift you are allowed to unwrap later — what does the first 24 hours best serve?
scenarios.prompt: Your manager says your updates are too detailed and stakeholders tune out. Best response?
scenarios.situation: Critical feedback lands in your review: your updates are too detailed; stakeholders tune out.
scenarios.title: The hard feedback
scenarios.why: Listen, clarify ('Can you show me an update that lost people?'), then sit with it before responding. The sting fades; the signal ('lead with the decision, bury the detail') is career gold. Instant defense teaches people to stop telling you things — the most expensive lesson in any career.

choices: Work when everyone else works; alignment matters most
Protect your peak hours for deep work and batch shallow work around them
Multitask through the day to stay responsive
Let your calendar fill and react
evidence: You solve hard problems 6-9am; afternoons are meetings and fog.
scenarios.hint: Your log already contains the answer — when is the fog, and when is the clarity?
scenarios.prompt: How should you restructure your day?
scenarios.situation: Your log shows hard problems get solved 6–9am; afternoons are fog and meetings.
scenarios.title: The energy audit
scenarios.why: Guard peak hours for deep work; batch email, admin, and meetings into the fog. Energy management beats time management — an hour at peak focus outproduces three foggy ones. Design the calendar around the energy, not the other way around.

choices: Treat it as the highest-value data you got: probe for examples and build a correction habit
Dispute it; one person's view isn't data
Ask HR to remove it from the record
Collect counter-opinions to outvote it
evidence: Peers: 'brilliant but interrupts; people stop bringing ideas.' You saw yourself as collaborative.
scenarios.hint: A blind spot is, by definition, invisible to you — so whose eyes do you need to borrow?
scenarios.prompt: 360 feedback reveals you interrupt and shut down ideas — news to you. Best move?
scenarios.situation: Peers describe you as brilliant but interruptive; you saw yourself as collaborative.
scenarios.title: The blind spot
scenarios.why: Blind spots are the highest-ROI feedback precisely because you cannot see them: ask for two specific examples, then build a visible correction ('I'm practicing a 3-second pause — call me on it'). Disputing it defends the ego and kills the data. The fix is behavioral and public.

choices: Build it quietly to delight them
Refuse; scope is scope
Acknowledge the need, show the tradeoff against the committed timeline, and offer a scoped path: now, next, or never
Escalate to their VP immediately
evidence: Deployment scope: SSO + data migration, 6 weeks. Week 3 request: custom reporting dashboard.
scenarios.hint: The customer is not wrong to want it — but yes has a price. How do you make the price visible without saying no?
scenarios.prompt: A customer stakeholder asks for a custom reporting dashboard mid-deployment. Best response?
scenarios.situation: Week 3 of a 6-week deployment (SSO + data migration), a stakeholder requests a custom reporting dashboard — not in the statement of work.
scenarios.title: The mid-deployment ask
scenarios.why: 'I can see why that matters. Here's what it does to the 6-week timeline — we can slot a light version in week 6, schedule the full build next, or cut something. Which tradeoff do you want?' Making tradeoffs visible respects the ask without silently blowing the commitment. Quiet yeses create failed deployments.

choices: Win a small, visible bet together: pick their hardest skeptic-approved problem and solve it fast
Send a whitepaper proving your approach
Go over their head to their manager
Match their skepticism with confidence and jargon
evidence: Customer's lead engineer openly doubts your architecture recommendation.
scenarios.hint: Trust is built in drops, not decks — what is the smallest proof that changes a skeptic's mind?
scenarios.prompt: The customer's lead engineer openly doubts your recommendation. Best move?
scenarios.situation: You are deployed at a customer site and their lead engineer distrusts your architecture recommendation.
scenarios.title: The skeptical engineer
scenarios.why: Engineers trust demonstrated competence, not slideware: pair on their gnarliest problem, ship a fix, let the result argue. One small win rewires the relationship; whitepapers and escalation deepen the divide. As the outsider, your credibility is earned in their codebase, not your deck.

choices: Fix it silently and mention it next week
Blame the customer's infrastructure to protect your product
Communicate early and often: impact, what you know, next update time — while you fix it
Wait until you have the full root cause before saying anything
evidence: Customer production down; your component implicated; 200 users affected.
scenarios.hint: In a customer incident, silence is read as the worst possible news — what cadence of communication calms a room?
scenarios.prompt: Their production is down and your component is implicated. Best approach?
scenarios.situation: At a customer site, production is down, your component is implicated, 200 users affected.
scenarios.title: The customer outage
scenarios.why: 'Impact: 200 users down. What we know: X. Next update in 20 minutes.' Then fix. Cadenced, honest updates convert panic into patience; silence converts it into escalation. Never blame the customer mid-incident — restore service first, do blameless analysis after, and own your component's part plainly.

choices: Document the runbooks, train two owners, and do a supervised handoff before you leave
Leave the wiki as-is; they can call you
Hand off to whoever is available on your last day
Keep the knowledge; it makes you indispensable
evidence: Deployment ends in 2 weeks; you rotate to the next customer.
scenarios.hint: Your deployment succeeds only if it survives your departure — what does 'done' actually mean here?
scenarios.prompt: You rotate off in two weeks. What does a real handoff look like?
scenarios.situation: Your deployment ends in two weeks and you rotate to the next customer.
scenarios.title: The clean handoff
scenarios.why: Done means two named owners can run it without you: updated runbooks, a recorded walkthrough, and a supervised week where they drive and you watch. Knowledge hoarding feels like job security but reads as a bus-factor risk — and customers remember who left them stranded.

choices: Pick the side with more political power
Find the shared goal both sides need, and frame your work as serving it
Treat it as not your problem; you're technical
Play the sides against each other to get clarity
evidence: Security wants lockdown; Product wants speed. Both claim your deployment.
scenarios.hint: Opposing stakeholders usually share a boss-level goal — what does both Security and Product ultimately answer to?
scenarios.prompt: Security wants lockdown, Product wants speed, both claim your deployment. Best move?
scenarios.situation: Two customer stakeholders pull your deployment in opposite directions.
scenarios.title: The stakeholder tug-of-war
scenarios.why: Find the shared goal — usually shipping safely to unblock revenue — and frame every decision as serving it: 'Here's how we get both: guardrails that let Product move fast inside them.' Refereeing power struggles burns you; translating between them makes you indispensable. Never pick a side in someone else's org chart.

choices: Build the full thing from your best guess
Wait for perfect requirements before starting
Prototype the riskiest assumption in days, put it in front of users, and converge
Write a 40-page spec to force clarity
evidence: Requirement: 'Make onboarding delightful.' That's the whole doc.
scenarios.hint: Vague requirements are a discovery problem, not a documentation problem — what is the cheapest way to learn what they actually want?
scenarios.prompt: The requirement is 'Make onboarding delightful.' Best first move?
scenarios.situation: You are handed a one-line requirement and a deadline.
scenarios.title: The vague requirement
scenarios.why: Prototype the riskiest assumption in days and watch a real user touch it — ten minutes of observation beats ten pages of guessing. Ambiguity resolves through contact with reality, not bigger specs. Each prototype narrows the cone of uncertainty; each spec review just polishes the guess.

choices: Build the product; great products sell themselves
Run 15-20 customer interviews about the problem before writing code
Launch a big marketing campaign on day one
Raise money first; funding validates the idea
evidence: 'An app that helps freelancers track scope creep.' No customers spoken to yet.
scenarios.hint: Ideas are cheap; problems are expensive — how do you know the problem is real before you build?
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first step?
scenarios.situation: You have an idea for an app but have spoken to zero potential customers.
scenarios.title: The unvalidated idea
scenarios.why: Fifteen to twenty interviews about the problem — not your solution — reveal whether the pain is real, frequent, and paid to fix. 'Would you pay for this?' asked after problem questions beats any pitch. Code is the most expensive way to learn nobody wants it.

choices: Include every feature you can imagine; more is more
Ship the smallest thing that tests the core value hypothesis
Polish for six months, then launch big
Build the admin panel first; you'll need it
evidence: V1 wishlist: 23 features, 4 integrations, mobile + web.
scenarios.hint: An MVP is an experiment, not a small product — what is the hypothesis, and what is the minimum that tests it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you scope the MVP?
scenarios.situation: Your V1 wishlist has 23 features, 4 integrations, and two platforms.
scenarios.title: The bloated MVP
scenarios.why: Define the one hypothesis ('freelancers will pay to track scope creep automatically') and ship the minimum that tests it — often a concierge or single-feature build. Every extra feature is unvalidated scope that delays learning. Cut until it hurts, then cut once more.

choices: Price at cost plus a small margin
Copy the competitor's price
Price on the value delivered, then test willingness to pay in interviews and pilots
Price as low as possible to win share
evidence: Your tool saves a 10-person agency ~$4k/month in write-offs.
scenarios.hint: Cost-plus ignores what the customer gains — what is the saving worth to them, and what fraction can you claim?
scenarios.prompt: How should you set the price?
scenarios.situation: Your tool saves a 10-person agency about $4k/month in write-offs.
scenarios.title: The pricing question
scenarios.why: Anchor on value: if you save $4k/month, $400–$800/month is an easy yes — then validate with real willingness-to-pay conversations and paid pilots. Cost-plus leaves money behind; race-to-the-bottom pricing starves you of the margin that funds support and growth. Price is a hypothesis; test it.

choices: Agree on vesting, roles, and decision rights in writing before real work starts
Split 50/50 on a handshake; trust is the foundation
Avoid the awkward conversation until there's revenue
Let the idea person take 80%; ideas matter most
evidence: Two cofounders, strong skills, no written agreement, 3 months in.
scenarios.hint: Founding agreements are cheapest when everyone still likes each other — what happens to a handshake split when someone leaves in month eight?
scenarios.prompt: What should you do before going further?
scenarios.situation: Two cofounders, three months in, no written agreement.
scenarios.title: The handshake split
scenarios.why: Four-year vesting with a one-year cliff, written roles, and decision rights — signed while everyone is friendly. Most cofounder breakups happen; vesting makes them survivable instead of fatal. The awkward conversation now prevents the company-killing one later.

choices: Spend faster to hit milestones that attract funding
Cut burn to extend runway and focus on the one metric that matters
Take a big loan to keep the team comfortable
Ignore it; startups are supposed to be close to the edge
scenarios.hint: Runway is time to learn — what buys you the most learning per dollar right now?
scenarios.prompt: Six months of cash left, revenue flat. Best move?
scenarios.situation: $180k in the bank, $30k/month burn, flat revenue.
scenarios.title: The shrinking runway
scenarios.why: Cut burn and focus the whole company on one survival metric — six months becomes nine, and focus beats frantic feature sprawl. Spending faster to 'hit milestones' usually just hits the wall sooner. Runway is measured in months of learning, not dollars of spending.

choices: Never pivot; persistence is everything
Pivot at the first sign of trouble
Pivot when the data shows the current path can't win: retention flat, acquisition costs rising, a adjacent segment pulling
Ask investors what to do
evidence: 18 months in: flat retention, CAC up 3x, but a side segment begs for a feature weekly.
scenarios.hint: Stubbornness and flakiness look identical in week one — what evidence separates them in month eighteen?
scenarios.prompt: When is a pivot the right call?
scenarios.situation: Eighteen months in: flat retention, acquisition costs tripled, but an adjacent segment keeps asking for one feature.
scenarios.title: The pivot question
scenarios.why: Pivot on evidence, not mood: the core loop isn't working (flat retention, rising CAC) while a real pull exists elsewhere. That is data, not defeat. Pivoting at the first dip is flakiness; never pivoting is ego. Let the metrics and the customers' revealed behavior decide.

choices: Put the ask in the subject line, keep it under 150 words, and make the action unmissable
Write a thorough background so nothing is missed
Send it late at night to show dedication
CC their manager for visibility
evidence: 47 unread; average skim time per email: 11 seconds.
scenarios.hint: You are writing for an 11-second skim — what survives the skim?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a professional email get a fast reply?
scenarios.situation: Your stakeholder has 47 unread emails and skims each for 11 seconds.
scenarios.title: The 11-second email
scenarios.why: Subject as the ask ('Approval needed: $2k vendor renewal by Friday'), body under 150 words, the action bold or first. Background goes in an attachment, not the email. CC'ing managers for visibility reads as escalation; thoroughness that nobody reads is just slow.

choices: Invite everyone who might care
Start with an agenda, end with owners and dates, and cancel it if there's no decision to make
Keep it open-ended so creativity flows
Record everything; the recording is the notes
evidence: 6 recurring meetings, no agendas, no notes, 14 hrs/week.
scenarios.hint: A meeting is expensive — multiply headcount by hourly cost. What earns that spend?
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix a meeting-heavy culture on your team?
scenarios.situation: Six recurring meetings, no agendas, no notes, fourteen hours a week.
scenarios.title: The meeting audit
scenarios.why: Every meeting needs an agenda, a decision to make, and ends with named owners and dates — otherwise cancel it. Notes are decisions and actions, not transcripts. The test: if the meeting disappeared, what decision would stall? If none, it was already waste.

choices: Complain to peers to build a coalition
Raise it privately with data and two options, seeking to understand first
Go over their head immediately
Say nothing; managers are always right
evidence: Your manager's plan will miss the deadline; you have the data.
scenarios.hint: Disagreement is a gift if it's wrapped right — what wrapping makes a manager able to hear it?
scenarios.prompt: You have data showing your manager's plan will miss the deadline. Best move?
scenarios.situation: Your manager's plan will miss the deadline and you can prove it.
scenarios.title: The disagreement
scenarios.why: Privately, with curiosity first: 'Can I pressure-test the timeline? Here's what the data shows — option A cuts scope, option B adds a contractor.' Private preserves face; data depersonalizes; options make you a problem-solver, not a critic. Public contradiction or silent compliance both fail — one burns trust, the other burns the deadline.

choices: Over-communicate outcomes: short weekly updates of shipped work and next steps
Stay heads-down; good work speaks for itself
Be constantly online to prove you're working
Send long daily activity logs
evidence: Fully remote team, async-first, manager in another timezone.
scenarios.hint: Remote managers can't see effort, only evidence — what evidence is cheapest for you to produce and most valuable for them?
scenarios.prompt: How do you stay visible and trusted on a remote team?
scenarios.situation: Fully remote, async-first team; your manager is in another timezone.
scenarios.title: The remote visibility
scenarios.why: A short weekly outcome update — shipped, learned, next — gives your manager everything they need to trust and advocate for you. Outcomes, not activity: nobody reads hour logs, and green-dot theater breeds resentment. In remote work, written communication IS the work.

choices: Do it; loyalty to the boss comes first
Refuse, document the request, and escalate through proper channels
Do it but keep no record
Quit on the spot without a word
evidence: Manager: 'Pull the full user export — including data we promised customers we'd never share — for my side project.'
scenarios.hint: Some lines can't be uncrossed — what protects you, the users, and the company at the same time?
scenarios.prompt: Your manager asks you to export customer data promised to stay private, for a side project. Best move?
scenarios.situation: Your manager asks for a full user export — including data promised never to be shared — for a personal side project.
scenarios.title: The unethical ask
scenarios.why: Refuse clearly, document the request contemporaneously, escalate via proper channels (skip-level, compliance, or legal). This protects users, the company, and you — 'my boss told me to' is not a defense. Quiet compliance makes you complicit; dramatic quitting without a record helps no one.

choices: Wait for your manager to notice and promote you
Build a growth plan: target skills, visible projects, and relationships with sponsors — reviewed quarterly
Job-hop every year for title bumps
Focus only on technical depth; soft skills don't matter
evidence: 'Strong technically. Limited visibility outside the team.'
scenarios.hint: Promotions go to people whose impact is known by decision-makers — what makes your impact known?
scenarios.prompt: Your review says 'strong technically, limited visibility.' Best response?
scenarios.situation: You want to grow but your impact is invisible outside your team.
scenarios.title: The growth plan
scenarios.why: Write it down: the skills the next level needs, one visible project per quarter that demonstrates them, and sponsors — senior people who know your work and speak for you in rooms you're not in. Mentors advise; sponsors advocate. Review the plan quarterly like any project, because your career is one.

concepts: Positioning gaps: never lie — background checks end careers faster than gaps do.

Principle: score offers on learning velocity, manager quality, financial stability, and trajectory — then let salary be one weighted factor, not the whole decision.

lessons.title: Career Launch - Core concepts
concepts: A resume is a marketing document, not a biography: one page per ten years of experience, bullets that quantify outcomes ('cut deploy time 40%'), and language mirrored from the posting so both applicant-tracking systems and humans see the match.
Treat the search as a pipeline - targets, applications, follow-ups, interviews - tracked in one spreadsheet. Follow up once after 7 to 10 days; silence is usually process, not verdict.
Behavioral interviews run on STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Prepare five stories (ownership, conflict, failure, scale, ambiguity) and adapt them; the Action is what gets scored.
Technical interviews score process: clarify requirements, state the brute force, optimize, then test edge cases - all out loud. A narrated O(n^2) beats a silent optimal solution.
A portfolio of two or three finished projects - README, live demo, honest 'what I'd do differently' - beats twenty half-done repos. Depth signals follow-through.
Negotiate once, with data: never accept on the spot, get the full written offer, compare total compensation, and counter against market ranges. Exploding deadlines are usually negotiable.

example.code:
comm -23 \
  <(tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' < posting.txt | grep -o '[a-z][a-z-]*' | sort -u) \
  <(tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' < resume.txt | grep -o '[a-z][a-z-]*' | sort -u) \
  | head -20
example.walkthrough: List distinctive words in the posting that never appear in the resume. The gap list shows which required skills and tools you are failing to signal before a human ever reads it - close the honest gaps, not all of them.

pitfalls: Common trap: one generic resume for 200 applications - tailor the top third (summary plus recent bullets) to each posting.
Common trap: answering 'tell me about yourself' with your life story - 60 to 90 seconds: present role, proof of fit, why this role.
Common trap: having no questions for the interviewer - ask about team goals, success metrics, and the hardest problem they face.
Common trap: treating the first offer as final - ask for written terms and time to decide; almost everything is negotiable once.

checklist: Research the company: mission, recent news, and the interviewers' backgrounds.
Prepare 3–5 STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result) in 60–90 seconds each.
Rehearse 'tell me about yourself' and 'why this role' out loud, not just in your head.
Prepare 3 smart questions to ask the interviewer about the team and the work.
Charge your devices; test camera, mic, and meeting link for virtual interviews.
Lay out professional attire the night before; plan to arrive 15 minutes early.
Bring printed copies of your tailored resume and a notepad.
Know your market salary range and your walk-away number before you walk in.
Send a thank-you email within 24 hours referencing something specific from the conversation.
Review your Career Strategy notes: positioning, gaps, and your value story.
Prepare one story that shows Interview Skills strength with a measurable result.
